problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 & \,∗\, \\ 0 & 1 & \,∗\, \\ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$

feedback.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \,∗\, & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \,∗\, & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 & \,∗\, & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first and third columns, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.
